spec.description: OHLC candles for one product over a time range, newest first. Each candle is a fixed six-column row rather than an object.

request.title: GetCandlesRequest
request.description: Which product, over which span, at which resolution.

product_id.description: Product id, such as `BTC-USD`. `products.list_products` returns it as `id`.

granularity.description: Bucket width in seconds: one minute, five, fifteen, one hour, six hours, one day. Any other value is rejected.

response.title: Candles
response.description: The candles in the span, newest first.

notes: Both bounds are inclusive, so the step is one second: a window whose `end` equalled the previous window's `start` would re-read the candle on the boundary. Confirmed against the live API -- `start=00:00Z&end=05:00Z` at hourly granularity returns six candles, not five.

No `size` is declared, and so no truncation guard is generated, because the endpoint has no page-size parameter to declare. That is safe here, and only because of how the exchange behaves: it *refuses* an over-wide range rather than truncating it. Measured at hourly granularity from a fixed historical start -- a 300-hour range (301 candles) is answered in full; 301 hours (302 candles) is HTTP 400, `granularity too small for the requested time range. Count of aggregations requested exceeds 300`. A caller that asks for too much finds out loudly, which is what the guard would otherwise have to do.

An earlier version of this note claimed the exchange silently caps a response at 300 candles. That was assumed rather than measured, and it is wrong. Kept here because the correction is the point: the difference between an API that truncates and one that refuses decides whether a client needs a guard at all, and it is not in the documentation either way.
